extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants, peer reviewers, Advisory Council members, and NIH extramural staff
extracted.subtask_description: Overview and standards for NIH initial and council peer review of grant and cooperative agreement applications, including core values, reviewer qualifications, scoring rules, review criteria, confidentiality/security, appeals, and procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two levels of NIH peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: An application must be approved by two levels of NIH peer review: (1) initial peer review conducted by a Scientific Review Group (SRG) assessing scientific and technical merit and producing a Summary Statement; and (2) Council review performed by Institute/Center (IC) National Advisory Councils or Boards which make recommendations on priority areas, policy, and funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial review is done by predominantly non-federal scientists appointed to SRGs; outcomes (Summary Statement) go to the IC and PD/PI. Councils include scientific members and public representatives; both reviews follow FACA and are conducted with a Designated Federal Official (DFO) present (SRO for SRG, Executive Secretary for Council). The IC Director makes final funding decisions considering staff and Council advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core values of NIH peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is guided by eight core values: expert assessment; transparency; impartiality; fairness; confidentiality; security; integrity; and efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These values form the foundation for laws, regulations, and policies governing NIH peer review and shape procedures for reviewer recruitment, scoring, confidentiality, COI management, security, handling misconduct, and process efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert assessment (reviewer qualifications and suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial review panels must have scientific expertise suitable for evaluating potential impact of the proposed work; reviewers are recruited based on expertise and stature, mature judgment, impartiality, and ability to work in a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of qualifications may include publication record, funding history, scientific achievements, and recommendations. Public representatives or individuals with technology transfer or accounting knowledge may be recruited when appropriate. Attention is given to balance in committee membership and appointments are made without discrimination on age, race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, disability, cultural, religious, or socioeconomic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency (use of published review criteria and Overall Impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are evaluated using established, published review criteria; only criteria published in the Funding Opportunity Announcement (FOA) may be used. Reviewers provide an Overall Impact score reflecting the likelihood the project will exert a sustained, powerful influence on the research field(s) involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall Impact is defined specifically for different mechanisms (e.g., for fellowships it reflects likelihood to enhance the candidate’s potential and commitment to an independent productive research career). Review criteria for mechanisms are stipulated in regulation and NIH policy; any additional criteria for special initiatives must be specified in the FOA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard scored review criteria for research applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard review criteria for research applications are: Significance; Investigators; Innovation; Approach; and Environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical scores on the nine-point scale are assigned to each of (at least) these five scored review criteria. Reviewers should assess these dimensions as defined in NIH policy and as appropriate to the FOA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard scored review criteria for fellowship applications
rubrics_metrics.description: For fellowship applications the review criteria include: Fellowship Applicant; Sponsor, Collaborators, and Consultants; Research Training Institutional Plan; Training Potential; and Environment & Commitment to Training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall Impact for fellowships is interpreted in the context of the fellow's training potential and the training environment. Additional or modified criteria for specific FOAs must be followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional review criteria (human subjects, inclusion, animals, biohazards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to assess additional criteria, as appropriate: Protections for Human Subjects; Inclusion of Women, Minorities, and Individuals Across the Lifespan; Vertebrate Animals; and Biohazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These additional criteria are evaluated where relevant to the proposed work and should be assessed according to NIH policy and regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional considerations that do not factor into Overall Impact score
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should comment on issues that do not factor into the Overall Impact score, including applications from foreign institutions, select agent research considerations, plans for sharing research resources, authentication of key biological variables, the budget request, and proposed project period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not part of the impact score, these considerations are documented in the Summary Statement and transmitted to PD/PIs and NIH staff for programmatic and policy decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring system and calculation of final impact score
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH uses a nine-point scoring scale (1 = highest impact, 9 = lowest impact). Final impact score is calculated as the average of individual reviewers’ scores multiplied by 10 (range 10–90).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical scores on the same nine-point scale are also assigned to each scored review criterion. For certain funding mechanisms, final impact scores are percentiled across different review panels to balance variable scoring behaviors among SRGs; a percentile approximates the percentage of applications that received better impact scores from the SRG during the past year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary Statement content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIH Summary Statement (written outcome of review) contains at a minimum written critiques and criterion scores from at least three reviewers, the final score or non-numerical outcome designation, and the meeting roster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may also contain a summary of the SRG discussion. Summary Statements are provided to the Advisory Council, PD/PI, appropriate NIH staff, and reviewers of subsequent resubmissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness through standard criteria and consistent processes
rubrics_metrics.description: All applications are evaluated using equivalent review processes and, for a given funding mechanism, standard review criteria (except for specified special initiatives), to ensure equitable evaluation across SRGs and Councils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of standard criteria and the scoring/percentiling approach helps ensure consistency when applications reviewed by different study sections are considered together at Council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and conflict-of-interest (COI) management
rubrics_metrics.description: Any circumstance that might introduce conflict of interest, appearance of COI, bias, or predisposition must be managed to avoid inappropriate influence. Bases for COI include financial interests, professional relationships, employment, memberships, personal relationships, and other interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must sign pre-meeting and post-meeting COI certifications; federal employees must adhere to Standards of Ethics. Federally-registered lobbyists may not participate. NIH separates review staff and program staff functions (no extramural staff serve as SRG reviewers; review staff do not participate in portfolio management in the same scientific area). One individual may not participate in both an application’s initial peer review and Council review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals of initial peer review — acceptable bases
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four acceptable bases for an appeal of initial peer review: evidence of bias on the part of one or more peer reviewers; conflict of interest on the part of one or more peer reviewers; lack of appropriate expertise within the SRG; and factual error(s) made by one or more reviewers that could have substantially altered the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals must be based on documentable flaws in the review process; in certain circumstances appeals can result in re-review of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality requirements and protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of review meetings are closed or partially closed to the public to protect confidential information; only federal employees with need-to-know, reviewers, and support contractors may attend. All discussions, application materials (except public-domain items), and information about COI and reviewer assignments are strictly confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must sign a confidentiality certification under penalty of perjury before access is granted. Reviewers must keep materials in secure locations, report lost/stolen materials immediately, and report breaches of security to the SRO/Executive Secretary or Review Policy Officer. NIH may take steps in response to violations (e.g., notifying institutions, terminating reviewer service, referring to OMA/OIG, pursuing suspension/debarment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Security of review communications and systems
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH uses secure electronic systems (IAR for SRG meetings, ECB for Council materials and votes, eRA Commons for applicant communications) with password protection and SRO authorization to protect sensitive application and review materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are responsible for secure handling of materials, must report potential security breaches, and NIH provides procedures for managing council business processes and Early Concurrence through ECB as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research integrity and handling allegations of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH extramural staff and reviewers participate in annual training on handling allegations of research misconduct; reviewers and Council members are instructed to report any suspicion or allegation of research misconduct to the DFO in strict confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each IC designates a Research Integrity Officer (RIO) to handle incoming allegations; DFOs contact RIOs as appropriate and may defer review pending authorities' deliberation. Allegations involving NIH funding with sufficient detail are forwarded to ORI for consideration/action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency and process improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH seeks to reduce time from submission to award and to reduce reviewer and staff burden by adopting electronic submission/handling (Grants.gov, IAR, eRA Commons), providing templates for written critiques, and instructing reviewers to provide brief, bulleted critiques rather than lengthy prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Web-based capabilities allow earlier identification of conflicts and faster assignment of replacement reviewers, direct electronic submission of critiques for Summary Statement production, and quicker posting of Overall Impact scores and Summary Statements to applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing competition (renewal) review adds progress assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: For renewals (continuing competition) the evaluation of scientific and technical merit also includes assessment of progress made during the previous award period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most grants are multi-year with annual progress reports; at renewal the SRG evaluates both the current proposal and documented progress to ensure accountability and continued merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation of global scientists
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists from around the globe are recruited as peer reviewers based on scientific and technical expertise, not official position, and accommodated through technologies that reduce need for travel (Internet Assisted Meetings, video conferencing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign reviewers are recruited for expertise; NIH uses emerging technologies to facilitate participation while maintaining review quality and security.
